item.title: morluto/rea
item.description:
Reverse engineer anything with agents, from app behavior down to native binaries.

https://rea.tools

English · 简体中文 · 繁體中文 · 日本語 · 한국어 · Türkçe · Русский · Tiếng Việt · ไทย · Deutsch · Español · Français · Українська · Polski · Português (Brasil) · العربية · فارسی · Bahasa Indonesia · Italiano · Ελληνικά · മലയാളം · Roman Urdu · Română

REA: Reverse Engineer Anything

One MCP for reverse engineering across binaries, applications, and runtime behavior.

See a feature you like. Understand how it works, down to the binary level.

Website · Guides · Showcases

Quick start · How REA works · What you can analyze · Showcases · Build RL environments · FAQ · Documentation

npx rea-agents setup

Important

Get REA from morluto/rea, rea.tools, or the rea-agents npm package. Follow the installation and release links from these official sources. A similar repository name or copied README does not establish that a download is official.





Join the Reverse Engineering Community
Discord · Q&A · Show and Tell

See a feature in an app that you want in your own product? Ask your agent to investigate it with REA. It can inspect the app without its source code, explain how the feature works, show the evidence, and build a version for your project.

REA connects your agent to tools for inspecting native binaries, JavaScript and Electron apps, .NET assemblies, and websites. You can also use the same tools from your terminal. Analysis runs locally, and results include the evidence and limitations behind each conclusion.

Setup registers REA with your agent and installs matching workflow instructions. Native analysis can use an existing Hopper, Ghidra, IDA or Kuna installation; setup can optionally install Hopper with approval. Static JavaScript analysis needs no native analysis engine.

Visit the REA website for setup instructions, illustrated guides, and real case studies.

Quick start

On Linux, Ghidra, JADX, firmware tool launches and static JavaScript/Electron analysis require a procps-compatible ps on REA's PATH for process ownership checks. Recovery steps are in docs/installation.md under "Linux owned-process prerequisite".

Set up your agent

With Node.js and npm installed, run:

npx rea-agents setup

Choose your agents, review the proposed changes, and approve them. Setup adds REA's MCP server and matching workflow instructions, with backups of existing configuration. Restart your agent afterward. Setup records the selected runtime and REA entry script directly. If acquired through a package runner, keep its cache entry available. Run package acquisition from a trusted directory outside the target project. Installation and recovery details are in the setup guide below.

Setup supports Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Grok Build and other agents. See installation and setup for provider configuration and manual MCP registration and Claude Code/Codex plugin installation.

MCP uses compact input schemas by default to reduce context overhead. Set REA_MCP_INPUT_SCHEMA_PROFILE=full in your MCP registration when you need the complete advertised field guidance and nested validation details. Both profiles keep the full tool set and canonical server validation. See "Compact input schema profile" in the MCP contracts guide.

Complete output schemas are advertised by default. If your client caps the complete tools/list frame, set REA_MCP_OUTPUT_SCHEMA_PROFILE=compact to bound each advertised output schema, or off to omit output schemas entirely. Both settings keep canonical server-side validation and complete structured results. See "Output schemas" in the MCP contracts guide.

Ask your agent

Understand how search works in the Notes app, show me the evidence, and build a
similar feature for my project.

Replace Notes with your target app and the feature you want to understand.

Use the terminal

Inspect an extracted JavaScript/Electron app directory or ASAR:

npx -y rea-agents@latest analyze-javascript-application /absolute/path/to/app --json

The result includes modules, imports, Electron boundaries and their evidence. Replace the path with your target, such as "D:/apps/example" on Windows.

To install the rea command for regular use:

npm install --global rea-agents
rea --help

For native analysis, configure a provider first. See the CLI and Evidence guide for native commands, provider selection, snapshots and scripting.

Update REA

REA changes quickly, and new releases include frequent bug fixes. Keep your installation up to date.

For a CLI installed with npm install --global or bun add --global:

rea update

rea --update is an alias for this verified workflow and accepts the same global output flags. Use rea update when combining it with other command controls.

Updater commands retain at most 4 MiB of stdout and stderr combined. Oversized metadata replies are rejected after the command exits; verbose installs continue with bounded diagnostics. Human progress output respects terminal backpressure and waits for submitted writes to finish.

Bun global updates require Bun 1.2.17 or later. With an older Bun release, upgrade Bun manually before running rea update.

To refresh your agent registrations and skill, run the setup command printed by the update.

If you use npx, update your agent setup with:

npx rea-agents@latest setup

Review the setup changes and restart your agent. For one-off CLI commands, use npx rea-agents@latest followed by the command. With Bun, use bunx rea-agents@latest in place of npx rea-agents@latest.

How REA works

Your agent calls REA through MCP to inspect the target and trace relevant code. REA returns findings with their evidence. The agent uses them to ask follow-up questions, explain the behavior, or write and test an implementation. CLI commands use the same workflows.

Open the full-size figure.

What you can analyze

REA requires Node.js 22.x (>=22.23.4), 24.x (>=24.22.1), or 26.12.1+, plus npm. Additional tools and host support depend on the target:

JEB projects Engine-backed project units, artifact digests and type/method pseudo-code A caller-started JEB client serving MCP, selected with REA_JEB_MCP_URL; JEB guide
Android resources Decoded manifest, string tables, locales and version facts Caller-supplied Apktool launcher; resource guide
Flutter apps Dart snapshot hash, per-ABI library digests and engine build provenance None (static APK parsing); Flutter guide
Firmware Regions, extraction results and native-analysis handoffs Binwalk / Unblob on Linux; firmware guide
Recorded packets Selected fields, repeated values, filters and decode-as rules Linux: TShark 4.x + prlimit; capture guide
Packet summaries Endpoints, DNS, TLS SNI, protocol distribution and HTTP requests Caller-supplied tshark and capinfos (Linux-verified); pcap guide
Recorded logic signals Decoder annotations, sample ranges and diagnostics Linux: sigrok-cli 0.7.2 + prlimit; signal recordings
Packages and resources File inventories, digests, plists, Apple bundle anatomy and extracted resources Artifact and JavaScript guide, Apple applications
Process behavior Terminal output, interactions, exit and filesystem observations, and run comparisons Linux/macOS with a native PTY; process capture
PyInstaller executables CArchive members, Python version, entry scripts and extracted bytecode None (static only); Python packaged applications

Static JavaScript and .NET inspection read the supplied files without running the application. Runtime capture runs or interacts with the selected target using your user permissions; each runtime guide describes its effects.

For offline native-binary inspection, REA also supports caller-supplied GNU objdump and Rizin. See the reverse-engineering tools guide for provider setup, CLI commands, and Evidence limitations. REA does not install or update either provider.

Native formats and host support vary by provider. See Hopper and Ghidra setup, the IDA guide (including an optional native MCP bridge), the Kuna decompiler guide, and experimental Windows Ghidra support. Ghidra also supports 16-bit DOS analysis. For large binaries, raise the provider's startup deadline with REA_GHIDRA_STARTUP_TIMEOUT_MS or REA_HOPPER_STARTUP_TIMEOUT_MS. For provider selection, see the CLI guide. Check release availability for features added since the latest npm release.

Showcases

DX-Ball: reconstruct a sound-pan calculation

Follow a sound call into its position-to-pan helper, inspect the instructions, and turn incomplete pseudocode into C. The reconstruction passes 3,205 original-x86 cases and reproduces all 63 compiled function bytes.

Read the case study · Reconstruction repository

Notion: trace the Electron clipboard bridge

Find the renderer's clipboard API, follow it through preload and IPC into the main process, and inspect the rich clipboard format.

Read the case study

TH04: recover a DOS bullet-ring calculation

Inspect the original PC-98 game's 16-bit instructions, recover the fixed and aimed angle calculations, and compare the reconstructed C++ with the historical compiler output.

Read the case study · Reconstruction repository

Build RL environments with REA

Record a web app session, turn its API into tools, and export an environment an AI agent can use. Run it with AgentEnv, then add tasks and reward checks for RL training or evaluation.

Read the guide · Watch the video

If you've used REA on something interesting, we'd love to see it. Share your case in an issue or a pull request, including the target, your question, how REA helped, and what you found.

Build RL environments

Give an AI agent a local environment to practice tasks such as finding an issue or creating a folder, without running the original app. Use it for reinforcement learning (RL) or to test how well an agent completes tasks.

REA turns recorded API requests and responses into tools the agent can call. The environment uses the recorded data and supports changes only when the recording confirms their effects.

With REA set up in your agent, replace the example URL and folder tasks below with your own:

Use REA to build an RL environment from my test web app at
http://127.0.0.1:3000.
Cover listing, creating, renaming, and deleting folders. You may create and
remove test folders. Leave existing data unchanged.
Save it in a folder named my-env. Check which operations work and tell me
how to run it.
Use the command line instead

Use these commands if you already have a file containing the app’s recorded browser requests and responses. Running the result also requires AgentEnv and Docker.

rea environment-build ./session.har ./my-env --name my-env --json
agent-env run ./my-env

REA exports a runnable environment with a basic test to check that it starts and responds. Use it with your RL framework to define task goals, add reward checks, and run training.

Build an environment · Environment reference · Watch the demo on X

FAQ

Which agents can use REA?

Any agent that supports local MCP servers. Setup configures the supported agents; other clients can use manual MCP registration.

Do I need a native analysis engine?

Deep native analysis uses Hopper, Ghidra, IDA or Kuna, depending on the target and operation. Static JavaScript and .NET inspection work without a native analysis engine. Setup can install Hopper after approval; Ghidra, IDA and Kuna use your existing installations. See provider setup for the options and their supported targets.

Do I need to start Hopper first?

REA starts Hopper when an operation needs it. On macOS, a first-run dialog may ask you to choose demo mode or activate your license. Complete that prompt in the same user session before your first CLI/MCP operation or unattended job. Open Hopper manually if needed. See Hopper startup and troubleshooting.

What does installing the skill from skills.sh do?

The skill supplies investigation instructions for your agent. Use npx rea-agents setup to register REA's MCP server and install the matching instructions, then restart your agent. See skill-only installation.

What code does REA return?

Native analysis returns pseudocode and assembly. JavaScript/Electron analysis recovers modules and their relationships. Your agent uses these findings to write and test an implementation; the showcases give worked examples.

Does REA upload my app?

REA analyzes targets locally. Your agent receives the tool results, and its model provider has its own data policy.

What should I do if I hit a bug?

Update first; a recent release may already fix it.

For a CLI installed with npm install --global or bun add --global:

rea update

For agent setup through npx:

npx rea-agents@latest setup

If you're using an agent, complete the setup refresh and restart it. Retry the same task. If the problem persists, open an issue with your REA version, target type, steps to reproduce and error output.

About

Tool for automatic executables porting to Linux and Windows.

The relinker-only build runs on macOS, including Apple silicon.

Web converter - files stay on your device.

Includes a relinker that converts executable to the target system's native format and implementations of system prx libraries suitable for dynamic linking. No emulation or separate runtime process.

Discord, Usage, Build instructions, Architecture, Technical debt of the project, code style conventions, contributing

Status

Progress history

* System libraries: percentage of the functions known to the project so far (declared in core/libs/prx), not of every PS5 system function. The total grows as more functions are declared.

Unsupported or unexpected states throw a C++ exception, usually std::runtime_error. An exception that nothing catches prints its what() to stderr and ends the process.

The shader recompiler successfully produces SPIR-V (validated via Spirv-Tools when built with ANYPS5_ENABLE_SPIRV_TOOLS).

Per-game status and test reports live in the Game bring-up discussions, one thread per title.

SDL-mapped game controllers are supported, including analog sticks and triggers. Keyboard and mouse controls can be configured with an anyps5-input.ini file. See input mapping for the supported devices and configuration format.

item.title: Nutlope/hallmark
item.description:
Anti-AI-slop design skill for Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex.

https://www.usehallmark.com/

Hallmark

A design skill for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and OpenCode that refuses to look AI-generated.

usehallmark.com  ·  fifty themes  ·  custom on request  ·  redesign and audit by name

Made by Together AI.

Hallmark holds a hard floor and then gets out of the way. It deals three themes from a catalog of fifty materials, builds the page around what the visitor came to do, and lints the result in a real browser against the tells that read as machine-made: the eyebrow above every heading, tracked-capital labels, one coloured word in a headline, a page of empty frames or nothing but photographs, a hero that misses its screen, an email sign-up at the end of every page, a form that says thanks without sending anything. A fresh-context reviewer gets the last word.

The gates come in tiers. The Floor never ships (contrast, focus, reduced motion, invented facts, a broken phone layout). Reflex gates are the defaults a model falls into; a build with a reason may overrule one on the record. Finish checks are craft detail that never blocks a ship.

New in v2

  • Fifty themes. Each is a material (paper, type, colour, surfaces, its own components and texture) with a picture of a finished page, and the build lays out its own page in it.
  • Built from the job. A booking page books, a shop sells, a newsletter subscribes: the action sits where the category puts it, and the page ends on it.
  • Custom. Ask for a custom page and Hallmark designs from your prompt alone, under the same rules and checks.
  • Your real product. Point it at a URL, a dev server or an app and it captures the screenshots itself.
  • Real photographs. 755 openly licensed photos, picked per subject and credited on the page.
  • Redesign and audit. /hallmark redesign <path> rebuilds a page and keeps its content and wiring; /hallmark audit <path> only reports.

Themes

Dusk
Closewise, bank reconciliation		 Cobalt
Relay, a webhook API		 Studio
Field Office, an identity studio		 Atelier
Maison Orla, a fragrance atelier		 Ribbon
Lull, a sleep sounds app
Furrow
Fieldbook, farm records		 Dose
Tandem, a family medication app		 Refract
Bellwater Lido, an outdoor pool		 Vantage
Swath, construction site scans		 Hedgerow
Five Mile Gin, a distillery

Ten of the fifty. A theme is a material, not a plan: it never says what a page contains or in what order, so two prompts in one theme make two different pages. Each is one file of at most 8 KB in references/themes/ with a picture beside it; a build reads exactly one. See them all at usehallmark.com.

Custom

Say custom and Hallmark drops the themes: no plan, no components, no palette recipe, only the floor, the gates and a short direction in direction.md to find one idea that only this client has and let it run the page.

How a build runs

  1. Pre-flight reads the project (fonts, palette, framework, a locked design.md) and asks once for the material: photos, screenshots, real numbers. Nothing is invented.
  2. scripts/theme.mjs deal offers three themes that fit the prompt and clear the log; draw deals the page's anatomy from its job.
  3. The hero is built alone, rendered and reviewed cold before the rest of the page exists.
  4. scripts/sloplint.mjs --render checks the page at eight widths, then a subagent reviews it with fresh eyes.

Each page is self-contained HTML and CSS, stamped in its first CSS comment with the decisions it took.

Redesign

Hallmark never starts on a design that already exists unless you name it:

/hallmark redesign ./src/app
/hallmark audit ./index.html

A full redesign keeps the content and the wiring and changes the system and the layout; say keep the layout for a restyle or polish for only the tells. sloplint --before records every link, field, handler and heading first, sloplint --kept fails the redesign if one went missing, and the handoff is a side-by-side before and after.

Install

npx skills add nutlope/hallmark -g

-g installs for every project; leave it off to install into the current one. Needs Node 18 or later. The browser checks (sloplint --render, screenshots) also need npm i -g puppeteer-core and Chrome; without them the static checks still run.

Harness Lands in Invoke
Claude Code ~/.claude/skills/hallmark /hallmark <prompt> or describe a new build
Codex CLI ~/.agents/skills/hallmark $hallmark <prompt> or describe a new build
Cursor finds the copies above /hallmark <prompt> or describe a new build
OpenCode finds the copies above /hallmark <prompt> or describe a new build
  • One harness only: npx skills add nutlope/hallmark -g --agent claude-code (or codex, opencode, cursor, github-copilot).
  • As a Claude Code plugin: /plugin marketplace add nutlope/hallmark, then /plugin install hallmark@hallmark (invoked as /hallmark:hallmark).
  • From a clone: node skills/hallmark/scripts/install.mjs validates every theme and reference before it copies; install-hook.mjs adds an edit-time Floor check to Claude Code.
  • Lint any page: node skills/hallmark/scripts/sloplint.mjs <file-or-dir> --render.
  • If it does not fire on its own, name it: use hallmark to build ....

Impeccable · frontend-design · Open Design · Kami · taste-skill · huashu-design · UI UX Pro Max · Emil Kowalski's skills · Web Interface Guidelines

item.title: cloudflare/security-audit-skill
item.description:
A coding-agent skill for multi-phase security audits with independently verified, machine-readable findings

security-audit

A coding-agent skill that turns your agent into a security auditor. It orchestrates isolated agents through reconnaissance, coverage-led hunting, candidate validation, structured output, independent record verification, and target-neutral reporting.

This is the skill that seeded Cloudflare's vulnerability discovery harness, described in Build your own vulnerability harness. The harness grew into a multi-stage, fleet-wide system; this skill is the single-repo starting point it evolved from.

What it does

The skill runs a structured audit in six phases:

  1. Reconnaissance -- map architecture, trust boundaries, input surfaces, prior evidence, and deterministic coverage in architecture.md and coverage-ledger.json.
  2. Coverage-led hunting -- assign isolated hunters from ledger units, record their checks, and use coverage critics to find gaps.
  3. Candidate validation -- give every unique candidate to a fresh verifier that tries to disprove it.
  4. Structured output -- write confirmed, needs_validation, and rejected records to findings.json and validate them against report-schema.json.
  5. Independent record verification -- fresh agents verify final source claims. Material replacements receive another independent verifier.
  6. Target-neutral reporting -- derive REPORT.md, FINDINGS-DETAIL.md, and NEEDS-VALIDATION.md from the verified records and coverage ledger.

The parent runs validate-coverage-ledger.cjs after creating the ledger and after each later ledger update. It runs validate-findings.cjs in Phase 4 and again after every Phase 5 replacement.

The verdicts are distinct: confirmed has a complete source trace and bounded observed result, needs_validation has an exact unresolved fact and no severity, and rejected records a disproved candidate.

Multiple runs against the same repo are additive. The skill uses prior ledgers and findings to target gaps, revalidate changed source, and carry forward current-source evidence without treating stale or unresolved work as covered.

Files

File Purpose
SKILL.md Setup, core principles, platform terminology, workflow overview, and audit anti-patterns
RECONNAISSANCE.md Phase 1 reconnaissance prompts and synthesis instructions
HUNTING.md Phase 2 orchestration, hunting methodology, and validation rules
ATTACK-CLASSES.md Core, wildcard, and obvious-things attack prompts
MEMORY-SAFETY-AND-BINARY.md Memory-safety, binary, and kernel hunting classes for native targets
AI-AND-LLM.md Prompt-injection, agent/tool, and output-handling hunting classes for LLM-backed targets
WEB-PROTOCOL-AND-AUTH.md HTTP request-framing, cache, and authentication-protocol hunting classes for HTTP-protocol and auth targets
CLIENT-SIDE.md DOM-injection, messaging-trust, UI-redress, and prototype-pollution hunting classes for client-side/browser targets
SUPPLY-CHAIN-AND-RELEASE.md Dependency, CI, release, signing, update, plugin, and extension hunting classes
CLOUD-AND-DEPLOYMENT.md IAM, infrastructure-as-code, container, serverless, ingress, and runtime-configuration hunting classes
PROTOCOLS-RPC-AND-MESSAGING.md RPC, serialization, queue, broker, webhook, and streaming-protocol hunting classes
RESOURCE-EXHAUSTION-AND-AVAILABILITY.md Shared resource, quota, queue, worker, and operator-spend hunting classes
DATA-ISOLATION-AND-LIFECYCLE.md Tenant isolation, cache, search, export, backup, migration, deletion, and restore hunting classes
DESKTOP-MOBILE-AND-LOCAL-IPC.md Native app, deep-link, webview, exported-component, helper, daemon, and local-IPC hunting classes
VALIDATION-AND-REPORTING.md Phases 3–6 candidate validation, structured output, record verification, and reporting
report-schema.json JSON schema for all three findings.json verdicts
validate-findings.cjs Zero-dependency validator for findings.json in Phases 4 and 5
validate-findings.test.cjs Findings-validator tests and producer-compatible fixture checks
validate-coverage-ledger.cjs Zero-dependency validator for coverage-ledger.json in Phases 1–5
validate-coverage-ledger.test.cjs Coverage-ledger validator tests

Installation

Install the skill with the Skills CLI:

npx skills add https://github.com/cloudflare/security-audit-skill \
  --skill security-audit

Use --global for a user-level installation:

npx skills add https://github.com/cloudflare/security-audit-skill \
  --skill security-audit \
  --global

Run npx skills --help for agent-selection and non-interactive options.

Usage

Start your coding agent in (or pointed at) the codebase you want to audit, then ask it to do a security audit:

security audit this codebase

find security vulnerabilities in ./src

do a security review, output to ~/audits/my-project

The skill activates automatically when the request matches its trigger (security audit, find vulnerabilities, pen-test the code, etc.). A direct codebase audit or pen-test request uses full audit mode. Security questions and focused vulnerability work use guidance mode unless you request report artifacts. In full audit mode, an unspecified output directory defaults to ~/security-audit-skill/<repo-name>/run-<N>. The workflow writes inside the target repository only when you explicitly select a directory that version control ignores.

Requirements

  • A coding agent with a model that supports tool use and parallel sub-agents
  • Node.js for the zero-dependency findings and coverage-ledger validators
  • An OS-enforced sandbox for target-controlled builds, tests, processes, browsers, emulators, fuzzers, and fixtures. It must disable external networking, use a sanitized allowlisted environment, enforce resource limits, and allow writes only to assigned scratch paths. Without these controls, the workflow keeps the lead as needs_validation instead of executing target code.

Design principles

  • Only confirm established boundary failures. Keep a source-grounded blocked lead as needs_validation with its exact unresolved fact.
  • Adversarial validation. The agent that checks a finding is never the agent that found it.
  • Severity requires impact. Likelihood x impact, not deviation from a checklist.
  • Defense-in-depth gaps are not vulnerabilities. If Layer A prevents the attack, the absence of Layer B is a hardening note.
  • Multiple runs improve coverage. In our test runs, a single run found roughly half of the vulnerabilities that repeated runs found in total.

Contact

Questions, feedback, or comparing notes on AI-driven security tooling: security-ai-research@cloudflare.com

item.title: heygen-com/hyperframes
item.description:
Write HTML. Render video. Built for agents.

https://hyperframes.heygen.com

Write HTML. Render video. Built for agents.

Studio | Quickstart | Showcase | Playground | Catalog | Docs | Discord

Download the desktop app: macOS · Windows · Linux (.deb)

HyperFrames is a free, open-source framework for turning HTML, CSS, media, and seekable animations into deterministic MP4 videos. Use it locally with the CLI, from AI coding agents with skills, or as the rendering core behind hosted authoring workflows.

The HyperFrames Studio app is free to use as well; its Pro plan adds HeyGen's top video, image, voice and music models.

Using Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, or another coding agent? Run npx hyperframes skills update once, then ask your agent to make a video.

Quick Start

With an AI coding agent

For Claude Code, install the versioned plugin:

claude plugin marketplace add heygen-com/hyperframes
claude plugin install hyperframes@hyperframes

To enable auto-update for the hyperframes marketplace, run claude in a terminal in your project. In Claude Code's terminal UI, run /plugin, then select Marketplaces → hyperframes → Enable auto-update. Afterward, use /hyperframes:hyperframes. See the plugin guide for Copilot, VS Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI, updates, and migration.

For standalone skills (including OpenCode), use:

npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The picker opens with nothing pre-selected — the Core Skills group is all you need; /slideshow, /remotion-to-hyperframes, /reverse-any-video, /style-sampling and /figma install on demand. Without the picker (a script or a CI job), npx hyperframes skills update installs exactly the core set, whereas skills add --all installs all 9 published skills. The six repo-internal skills under .claude/skills / .agents/skills are excluded by default. For the full published set use npx hyperframes skills.

skills add resolves the skills.sh registry blob, which can lag main by hours. npx hyperframes skills update installs the skills from the release tag that matches your CLI version, so they match the CLI that runs them.

Run project-local installs from your video project's directory. From a HyperFrames checkout, use npx hyperframes skills update for a global install instead: a project-local installer target can overlap the tracked skills/ source and overwrite uncommitted edits. See contributor setup.

Try a prompt like:

Using /hyperframes, create a 10-second product intro with a fade-in title, a background video, and subtle background music.

The skills teach agents the HyperFrames production loop: plan the video, write valid HTML, wire seekable animations, add media, lint, preview, and render. They work with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, IBM Bob, and other coding agents that support skills.

Skills

HyperFrames ships 9 skills. Make any video by asking for it; the /hyperframes skill carries the contract and the references (film, captions, overlays, motion, look). Read it first.

For standalone installation, default to the core set (/hyperframes, /hyperframes-cli, /hyperframes-registry, /media-use). npx hyperframes skills update installs exactly that from anywhere; the interactive picker (npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes) lists it as the "Core Skills" group, nothing pre-selected. The picker is interactive-only — a non-interactive or agent run without --skill installs all 9. Use npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes --all to install the complete published set deliberately (skips the picker), or npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes --skill <name> for just one (bare name, no leading /).

Standalone installs stay lean after that: npx hyperframes init installs the core set only when it is missing and never touches a skill you already have (npx hyperframes skills update refreshes them, and never removes one); /figma, /slideshow, /remotion-to-hyperframes and /reverse-any-video install on demand with npx hyperframes skills update <name>. Nothing re-pulls the full set behind your back.

Plugin packages

Plugins bundle the full skill catalog and use their agent's update manager. bun run package:agent-plugin builds the committed portable ZIP, source metadata, and SHA-256 checksum. See the maintainer checklist.

Upload to Codex

Build the upload-ready Codex plugin archive from the committed HEAD version of the manifest, brand assets, and skills:

bun run package:codex-plugin

This writes dist/hyperframes-plugin.zip with a hyperframes/ root folder and fails if the archive exceeds Codex's 100 MB upload limit.

Core set

Skill Use when
/hyperframes Read first for any request to make, edit, animate or render a video, motion graphic, captions or overlays with HyperFrames (HTML rendered to video). Holds the render contract and the work loop, and points to the references for format, motion, look, captions, whole films and storyboards.
/hyperframes-cli The HyperFrames CLI by job — scaffold, check, look at frames, edit the timeline, preview, render locally or in the cloud, publish, project history — plus reading its JSON and recovering from build or render failures.
/hyperframes-registry About 450 ready-made blocks and components installed as editable source — transitions, overlays, titles, kinetic type, captions, charts, maps, 3D, camera moves. Use before hand-building any named visual; also for hyperframes add and catalog.
/media-use Get or make any media for a video — music, sound effects, images, icons, logos, voiceover, avatar and generated video, transcripts, cutouts, colour grades and looks — with HeyGen or free local tools, and mix placed audio. Also for footage that looks dark, flat or dull.

On demand

Skill Use when
/figma Bring Figma into a video — rendered assets, brand tokens, components, storyboard frames as reconstructed motion, shaders and connector-assisted motion. Use when you paste a figma.com link.
/slideshow A presentation, pitch deck or interactive deck — discrete slides, fragment reveals, branching, hotspot navigation, presenter mode with speaker notes. Output is a navigable deck, not a rendered MP4.
/remotion-to-hyperframes Bringing existing video code or footage into HyperFrames (Remotion first; also Motion Canvas, Lottie, Three.js, canvas, other tools' renders), verified frame by frame.
/reverse-any-video Rebuilding any video file as an editable HyperFrames project (motion graphics, talking heads, live action, AI-generated footage), checked frame by frame against the original. HyperFrames Pro.
/style-sampling Making a new episode on your topic in one of five proven styles: Collage Explainer, Finance Explainer, Animated Science Explainer, 3D Brand Explainer, 3D True Crime. HyperFrames Pro.

For visual design handoff workflows, see the Claude Design guide and Open Design guide.

Manually with the CLI

npx hyperframes init my-video
cd my-video
npx hyperframes preview      # preview in browser with live reload
npx hyperframes render       # render to MP4

Requirements: Node.js 22+, FFmpeg

What You Can Build

Need ideas? Browse the Showcase for finished videos you can watch, read, run, and remix.

  • Product launch videos and feature announcements
  • PR walkthroughs with animated code diffs, narration, and captions
  • Data visualizations, chart races, and map animations
  • Social videos with kinetic captions, overlays, and music
  • Docs-to-video, PDF-to-video, and site-tour explainers
  • Reusable motion graphics for automated content pipelines

Frame.md

frame.md — your design system, ready for video.

Every brand has a design.md. None of them were written for a camera. frame.md is the missing translation layer: it takes your web-context design spec and inverts it for the frame — the same tokens, the same rules, but rewritten so an AI agent can compose a promo video without guessing at scale or reaching for web chrome.

The output is a DESIGN.md superset your whole toolchain can read. Atoms stay sacred. Composition stays free. Numbers come from the script.


Biennale Yellow
BlockFrame

Blue Professional
Bold Poster

Broadside
Capsule

Cartesian
Cobalt Grid

Coral
Creative Mode

Browse and remix them all at hyperframes.studio/design.

How It Works

Define a video as HTML. Add data attributes for timing and tracks. Use GSAP, CSS, Lottie, Three.js, Anime.js, WAAPI, or your own frame adapter for seekable animation.

<div id="stage" data-composition-id="launch" data-start="0" data-width="1920" data-height="1080">
  <video
    class="clip"
    data-start="0"
    data-duration="6"
    data-track-index="0"
    src="intro.mp4"
    muted
    playsinline
  ></video>

  <h1 id="title" class="clip" data-start="1" data-duration="4" data-track-index="1">Launch day</h1>

  <audio
    data-start="0"
    data-duration="6"
    data-track-index="2"
    data-volume="0.5"
    src="music.wav"
  ></audio>

  <script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/gsap@3/dist/gsap.min.js"></script>
  <script>
    const tl = gsap.timeline({ paused: true });
    tl.from("#title", { opacity: 0, y: 40, duration: 0.8 }, 1);
    window.__timelines = window.__timelines || {};
    window.__timelines.launch = tl;
  </script>
</div>

Preview instantly in the browser. Render locally or in Docker. The renderer seeks each frame in headless Chrome and encodes the result with FFmpeg, so the same input produces the same video.

HyperFrames Stack

HyperFrames is the open-source rendering engine, plus a growing set of tools around HTML-native video creation.

Piece Status What it does
CLI Available Scaffold, preview, lint, inspect, and render local video projects
Core / Engine / Producer Available Parse compositions, drive headless Chrome, encode video, and mix audio
Catalog Available Reusable blocks and components for transitions, overlays, captions, charts, maps, and effects
Agent skills Available Teach coding agents the video-production patterns that generic web docs miss
Studio Available, evolving Browser surface for previewing and editing compositions
AWS Lambda rendering Available Deploy a distributed render stack and drive renders from your laptop or CI
hyperframes.studio Available Community playground for previewing, iterating, sharing, and rendering HTML-native video projects
frame.md Available Invert your design system for the camera — a DESIGN.md superset an agent can compose video from

Catalog

Install ready-to-use blocks and components:

npx hyperframes add flash-through-white   # shader transition
npx hyperframes add instagram-follow      # social overlay
npx hyperframes add data-chart            # animated chart

Browse the catalog at hyperframes.heygen.com/catalog.

Why HyperFrames?

  • HTML-native: compositions are HTML files with data attributes. No React requirement, no proprietary timeline format.
  • Agent-friendly: agents already write HTML, and the CLI is non-interactive by default.
  • Deterministic: same input, same frames, same output. Built for CI, regression tests, and automated rendering.
  • No build step: an index.html composition plays as-is and can be previewed directly in the browser.
  • Adapter-based animation: bring GSAP, CSS animations, Lottie, Three.js, Anime.js, WAAPI, or a custom runtime.
  • Open source: Apache 2.0 license, with no per-render fees or commercial-use thresholds.

HyperFrames vs Remotion

HyperFrames is inspired by Remotion. Both tools render video with headless Chrome and FFmpeg. The main difference is the authoring model: Remotion's bet is React components; HyperFrames' bet is plain HTML that humans and agents can both write easily.

HyperFrames Remotion
Authoring HTML + CSS + seekable animation React components
Build step None; index.html plays as-is Bundler required
Agent handoff Plain HTML files JSX / React project
Library-clock animations Seekable, frame-accurate via adapters Wall-clock animation patterns need care
Distributed rendering Local and AWS Lambda render paths Remotion Lambda, mature cloud renderer
License Apache 2.0 Source-available Remotion License

item.description:
https://t3.codes

T3 Code

T3 Code is an "agent harness control surface". It enables control of the agents on your machine with a best-in-class mobile app (iOS, Android), web app and Electron-based desktop app.

Works with your subscriptions on Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Grok Build, OpenCode, Google Antigravity, and fx. If they're set up on your computer, T3 Code can control them.

"Wait, what are you selling me?"

Nothing. We built T3 Code because we wanted the best possible development experience with agents. We were inspired by existing solutions like the Codex desktop app, Conductor, Claude Desktop and Cursor Glass, but none met our bar.

We wanted something performant, remote-ready, and truly open. If we ever go the wrong direction, we want you to have everything you need to fork and build the editor that you want.

Installation

Warning

T3 Code currently supports Codex, Claude, Cursor, Grok Build, OpenCode, Antigravity, and fx. Install and authenticate at least one provider before use:

  • Codex: install Codex CLI and run codex login
  • Claude: install Claude Code and run claude auth login
  • Cursor: install Cursor CLI and run agent login
  • Grok Build: install Grok Build CLI and run grok login
  • OpenCode: install OpenCode and run opencode auth login
  • Antigravity: enable it in Settings, then use Install Antigravity and Sign in with Google. No CLI is required.
  • fx: install fx and run fx login on the machine running the T3 Code server (setup guide)

Command line

curl -fsSL https://t3.codes/install.sh | sh

On Windows, in PowerShell:

irm https://t3.codes/install.ps1 | iex

Then run t3 to start the server and open the local web app. t3 service install keeps it running in the background, t3 update moves to a newer release, and t3 --help has the full reference.

To try it once without installing, run npx t3@latest instead.

Desktop app

Install the latest version of the desktop app from GitHub Releases, or from your favorite package registry:

Windows (winget)

winget install T3Tools.T3Code

Windows (scoop)

scoop install extras/t3code

macOS (Homebrew)

brew install --cask t3-code

Debian, Ubuntu (.deb)

Download the .deb from GitHub Releases, then:

sudo apt install ./T3-Code-*.deb

Arch Linux (AUR)

Stable:

yay -S t3code-bin

Nightly:

yay -S t3code-nightly-bin

The AUR packaging is maintained in this repository under packaging/aur.

Nix (nixpkgs)

nix profile add github:NixOS/nixpkgs/nixos-unstable#t3code

The package is maintained in nixpkgs and includes the desktop app (t3code-desktop) and the t3 command. See Nix installation for NixOS configuration and updates.

Some notes

We are very very early in this project. Expect bugs.

We are (mostly) not accepting contributions yet. Small fixes may be considered. Big features will not be.

Documentation

Full docs live in docs/. There's no docs site yet.

  • FAQ
  • Install and first run
  • Permission modes
  • Keyboard shortcuts
  • Project settings
  • Appearance preferences
  • Remote access from a phone or another machine
  • Connect Claude Code, Codex, ChatGPT and other agents over MCP
  • Keeping app and server in sync
  • Source control integrations
  • Multiple accounts: Codex · Claude
  • Run T3 Code as a background service

Building from source? Start at docs/internals/overview.md.

If you REALLY want to contribute still.... read this first

Install vp

T3 Code uses Vite+ so you'll need to install the global vp command-line tool.

macOS / Linux

curl -fsSL https://vite.plus | bash

Windows

irm https://vite.plus/ps1 | iex

Checkout their getting started guide for more information: https://viteplus.dev/guide/

Install dependencies

vp i

Read CONTRIBUTING.md before reporting a bug or opening a PR.

Have a feature request? Start an Ideas discussion.

Need support? Join the Discord.

item.title: thedotmack/claude-mem
item.description:
Persistent Context Across Sessions for Every Agent – Captures everything your agent does during sessions, compresses it with AI, and injects relevant context back into future sessions. Works with Claude Code, OpenClaw, Codex, Gemini, Hermes, Copilot, OpenCode + More

https://claude-mem.ai


       

🇨🇳 中文 • 🇹🇼 繁體中文 • 🇯🇵 日本語 • 🇵🇹 Português • 🇧🇷 Português • 🇰🇷 한국어 • 🇪🇸 Español • 🇩🇪 Deutsch • 🇫🇷 Français • 🇮🇱 עברית • 🇸🇦 العربية • 🇷🇺 Русский • 🇵🇱 Polski • 🇨🇿 Čeština • 🇳🇱 Nederlands • 🇹🇷 Türkçe • 🇺🇦 Українська • 🇻🇳 Tiếng Việt • 🇵🇭 Tagalog • 🇮🇩 Indonesia • 🇹🇭 ไทย • 🇮🇳 हिन्दी • 🇧🇩 বাংলা • 🇵🇰 اردو • 🇷🇴 Română • 🇸🇪 Svenska • 🇮🇹 Italiano • 🇬🇷 Ελληνικά • 🇭🇺 Magyar • 🇫🇮 Suomi • 🇩🇰 Dansk • 🇳🇴 Norsk

Your coding agent forgets everything between sessions. Claude-Mem remembers for it.

Quick Start • How It Works • Search Tools • Documentation • Configuration • Troubleshooting • License

Every new session, your agent starts from zero. It re-reads the same files, re-asks the same questions, and walks back into mistakes you already fixed together.

Claude-Mem runs a second agent beside it that takes notes while it works. The next session starts with a short index of what matters, and pulls in the details only when it needs them. Works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode and 11 more agents. Copilot CLI, Goose, Roo Code and Warp can search your memory, but their sessions aren't recorded.

Quick Start

Installing for someone as an AI agent? Run npx claude-mem install --runtime worker on their computer in an interactive terminal (enable PTY in your shell tool). It first asks in the terminal which agents to set up and, for Claude Code, whether to disable native auto-memory (and whether to overwrite an existing install). Relay each question to the user and type their answer, or pass --ide <id> to skip the first one. Keep the installer running. When it prints Continue setup in your browser, open that URL in the user's browser if the installer hasn't already opened it. Let the user go through setup and make their own choices, including the usage-analytics question the installer may ask at the end. If you can't run an interactive terminal on their computer, give them the command to run locally.

npx claude-mem install

The installer finds the agents on your machine and asks which ones to set up. Then just start working: observations stream in from your first prompt, and your second session in a project opens with memory from the first. (Copilot CLI, Goose, Roo Code and Warp get memory search only, so their sessions don't add to it.)

The installer sets everything up first, then asks you to sign in to claude-mem in your browser (email magic link — no card required). Signing in provisions a memory key for your account and unlocks the claude-mem observer with a 30 Day Free Trial: memory runs off-plan, so you get up to 100% more usage from your plan. When the free trial ends, memory automatically falls back to your Anthropic plan unless you subscribe. After sign-in you pick your memory provider — the claude-mem observer, your own OpenRouter or Gemini key, or your Anthropic plan.

Prefer to skip the sign-in? Pass an explicit --provider flag, set CLAUDE_MEM_ONLINE_OPTIN=false, or run in CI/non-interactive shells — the installer completes without any account interaction.

Your memory lives in ~/.claude-mem on your machine. Cloud sync is opt-in. Anonymous usage analytics are on by default; npx claude-mem telemetry disable turns them off (what's collected).

Or install from the plugin marketplace inside Claude Code:

/plugin marketplace add thedotmack/claude-mem

/plugin install claude-mem

Restart Claude Code. Context from previous sessions will automatically appear in new sessions.

Note: Claude-Mem is also published on npm, but npm install -g claude-mem installs the SDK/library only — it does not register the plugin hooks or set up the worker service. Always install via npx claude-mem install or the /plugin commands above.

Other agents

npx claude-mem install covers every supported agent. To set up one agent directly, pass --ide.

OpenCode (1.3.4 or later, including OpenCode 2). Restart OpenCode after installing.

npx claude-mem install --ide opencode

T3 Code (Codex and Claude Code providers). The installer discovers T3 Code's enabled providers, registers native Claude-Mem plugins in their configured homes, and supports T3-managed Codex. Restart T3 Code, trust the provider's hooks when prompted, and start a new thread. See the T3 Code integration guide for custom server settings, status, and removal.

npx claude-mem install --ide t3code

Antigravity CLI (setup guide):

npx claude-mem install --ide antigravity

OMP (Oh My Pi):

npx claude-mem install --ide omp

Pi and DeepSeek Harness use the worker runtime. See native harness setup for capture, recall, and troubleshooting.

npx claude-mem install --ide pi
npx claude-mem install --ide dsh --dsh-profile tui

Grok Bot: see Grok Bot below.

npx claude-mem install --ide grok-bot

The full list of --ide values is in npx claude-mem --help.

Grok Bot

Grok Bot has no host hooks, so we watch the chat log files. Default is CMEM Pro, the hosted memory. Local observer is opt-in: --provider host. Installing this plugin does not install Cursor.

Awareness push pilot (LFG + Orifice): needle observations (decision, bugfix, security_alert, sensitive) are appended as dated - YYYY-MM-DD [awareness] … lines into that bot's memory/log/YYYY-MM.md. Grok Bot already re-reads the log from disk. This does not write profile.md, user-memory, or project memory. Disable with CLAUDE_MEM_GROK_BOT_AWARENESS_ENABLED=false.

🦞 OpenClaw Gateway

Install claude-mem as a persistent memory plugin on OpenClaw gateways with a single command:

curl -fsSL https://install.cmem.ai/openclaw.sh | bash

The installer handles dependencies, plugin setup, AI provider configuration, worker startup, and optional real-time observation feeds to Telegram, Discord, Slack, and more. See the OpenClaw Integration Guide for details.

What You Get

  • 🧠 The next session starts where the last one left off. Each session opens with a compact index of past observations, layered so the agent opens full details only when it needs them, and the header can show what each layer costs in tokens.
  • 🔍 Find anything you worked on. The mem-search skill searches your project history in three steps (index, timeline, details), so the agent spends tokens only on what it opens.
  • 🖥️ Watch it work, and keep track of yours. My Work shows live requests, progress, human handoffs and a saved review queue at the worker URL printed on startup. Guide. Memory, sessions and settings remain at /viewer.
  • 👥 Share with your team, if you want. TeamBrain is an optional shared workspace beside My Work, with real team work lists, member attribution and linked findings. Each person chooses what to share; personal requests and review notes stay separate. Set up a team.
  • 💻 Search from Claude Desktop. Search your memory from Claude Desktop conversations.
  • 🔒 Keep secrets out. Wrap anything in <private> tags and it never gets stored.
  • 🖼️ Screenshots (opt-in, off by default). Keep converted copies of tool screenshots under ~/.claude-mem/media-v1/, upload them to cmem.ai only when cloud sync is on, and send them to the observer model only when image inference is separately enabled (details).
  • ⚙️ Choose what gets injected. Fine-grained settings for what context a new session starts with.
  • 🤖 Nothing to remember to do. It runs on its own once installed.
  • 🔗 Point back to past work. Every observation has an ID you can cite through the worker API or open in the web viewer.

Documentation

📚 View Full Documentation - Browse on official website

Getting Started

  • Installation Guide - Quick start & advanced installation
  • Usage Guide - How Claude-Mem works automatically
  • Search Tools - Query your project history with natural language
  • Cloud Sync - Back up your memory to cmem.ai — no daemon, the worker syncs on write

Best Practices

  • Context Engineering - AI agent context optimization principles
  • Progressive Disclosure - Philosophy behind Claude-Mem's context priming strategy

Architecture

  • Overview - System components & data flow
  • Architecture Evolution - The journey from v3 to v5
  • Hooks Architecture - How Claude-Mem uses lifecycle hooks
  • Hooks Reference - Every hook entry explained
  • Worker Service - HTTP API & Bun management
  • Database - SQLite schema & FTS5 search
  • Search Architecture - Hybrid search with Chroma vector database

Configuration & Development

  • Configuration - Environment variables & settings
  • Development - Building, testing, contributing
  • Troubleshooting - Common issues & solutions

How It Works

  1. Your agent works. Hooks in your agent hand each tool call (what it reads, edits and runs) to a small local worker.
  2. The observer takes notes. A second agent turns that activity into short observations, and writes a summary when the session ends.
  3. The next session starts with them. When a session starts, your agent gets a compact index of the observations that matter for this project, and fetches full details only when it needs them.

Memory injection starts on your second session in a project. To front-load a whole repo instead, run /learn-codebase (~5 minutes on a typical repo, optional).

See Architecture Overview for details.

How it fits together

For contributors, the main parts and where they live:

  • The claude-mem command (src/npx-cli/index.ts): install, repair, doctor, start, search and the rest. The installer puts a small launcher on PATH so hooks can run claude-mem directly.
  • Hooks (src/cli/hook-command.ts, one adapter per agent in src/cli/adapters/): each agent event runs one shell-free command, such as claude-mem hook claude-code <event>. For Claude Code that's Setup (claude --init / --maintenance), SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure, Stop, SubagentStop and SessionEnd.
  • The worker (src/services/worker-service.ts, routes in src/services/worker/http/routes/): a local HTTP service managed by Bun. It takes tool activity from the hooks, runs the observer, and serves the viewer and search.
  • The observer (prompts in src/sdk/, one provider per model source in src/services/worker/, such as ClaudeProvider.ts and OpenRouterProvider.ts): turns tool activity into observations and summaries.
  • Storage (src/services/sqlite/): SQLite at ~/.claude-mem/claude-mem.db holds sessions, observations and summaries. Chroma adds semantic search on top of SQLite's keyword search (src/services/worker/search/).
  • Context (src/services/context/): builds the block a new session starts with.
  • Search (src/servers/mcp-server.ts, plugin/skills/mem-search/): the MCP tools and the mem-search skill that drives them.
  • The viewer (src/ui/viewer/ at /viewer, src/ui/my-work/ at /): memory, sessions and settings, plus My Work.
  • The built plugin (plugin/): written by npm run build; edit src/, not the generated scripts.

The words we use for each of these, and the story they tell, are in docs/story.md.

MCP Search Tools

Search runs through three MCP tools in a token-efficient three-step workflow. The mem-search skill drives it for you:

The three steps:

  1. search - Get compact index with IDs (~50-100 tokens/result)
  2. timeline - Get chronological context around interesting results
  3. get_observations - Fetch full details ONLY for filtered IDs (~500-1,000 tokens/result)

Step by step:

  • Your agent uses MCP tools to search your memory
  • Start with search to get an index of results
  • Use timeline to see what was happening around specific observations
  • Use get_observations to fetch full details for relevant IDs
  • ~10x token savings by filtering before fetching details

Available MCP Tools:

  1. search - Search memory index with full-text queries, filters by type/date/project
  2. timeline - Get chronological context around a specific observation or query
  3. get_observations - Fetch full observation details by IDs (always batch multiple IDs)

Example Usage:

// Step 1: Search for index
search(query="authentication bug", type="bugfix", limit=10)

// Step 2: Review index, identify relevant IDs (e.g., #123, #456)

// Step 3: Fetch full details
get_observations(ids=[123, 456])

The worker also offers tools for code navigation (smart_search, smart_outline, smart_unfold), saving a note on purpose (save_memory) and tracking work in progress. See Search Tools Guide for detailed examples.

System Requirements

  • Node.js: 20.19 or later in the 20.x line, or 22.12 or later
  • A supported agent: Claude Code (latest, with plugin support) or any agent in Other agents
  • Bun: JavaScript runtime and process manager (auto-installed if missing)
  • uv: Python package manager for vector search (auto-installed if missing)
  • SQLite 3: For persistent storage (bundled)

Windows Setup Notes

If you see an error like:

npm : The term 'npm' is not recognized as the name of a cmdlet

Make sure Node.js and npm are installed and added to your PATH. Download the latest Node.js installer from https://nodejs.org and restart your terminal after installation.

Claude Code hooks do not need Git Bash. Each hook runs claude-mem directly, and npx claude-mem install places that launcher at %LOCALAPPDATA%\claude-mem\bin\claude-mem.exe and adds the folder to your user Path. Restart your terminal or IDE afterwards so Claude Code picks up the new Path. If hooks report Executable not found in $PATH: "claude-mem", run npx claude-mem doctor and see Troubleshooting.

Configuration

Settings are managed in ~/.claude-mem/settings.json (auto-created with defaults on first run). Configure AI model, worker port, data directory, log level, and context injection settings.

To include observations from every harness in Claude Code and Codex SessionStart context, set "CLAUDE_MEM_SESSION_START_INCLUDE_ALL_SOURCES": "true" in that file, or enable Include all sources at session start in the viewer settings. The default is "false", which limits startup context to the current harness. The observation count limit still applies across the selected sources.

See the Configuration Guide for all available settings and examples.

Mode & Language Configuration

Claude-Mem supports multiple workflow modes and languages via the CLAUDE_MEM_MODE setting.

This option controls both:

  • The workflow behavior (e.g. code, chill, investigation)
  • The language used in generated observations

How to Configure

Edit your settings file at ~/.claude-mem/settings.json:

{
  "CLAUDE_MEM_MODE": "code--zh"
}

Modes are defined in plugin/modes/. To see all available modes locally:

ls ~/.claude/plugins/marketplaces/thedotmack/plugin/modes/

Available Modes

Mode Description
code Default English mode
code--chill Records fewer observations, keeping only what would be painful to rediscover
code--[lang] Same as code, with observations and summaries written in another language

Built-in language codes: ar, bn, cs, da, de, el, es, fi, fr, he, hi, hu, id, it, ja, ko, nl, no, pl, pt-br, ro, ru, sv, th, tr, uk, ur, vi, zh. For example, code--ko writes observations and summaries in Korean.

See Modes for each language's name, the email investigation mode, and custom modes.

Note: All of these modes are built in. No additional installation or plugin update is required.

After Changing Mode

Restart Claude Code to apply the new mode configuration.

Development

See the Development Guide for build instructions, testing, and contribution workflow.

Troubleshooting

Start with npx claude-mem doctor. It checks Bun, uv, the hook launcher and the worker, and tells you what to fix.

See the Troubleshooting Guide for common issues and solutions.

Bug Reports

Create comprehensive bug reports with the automated generator:

cd ~/.claude/plugins/marketplaces/thedotmack
npm run bug-report

Contributing

Contributions are welcome! Please:

  1. Fork the repository
  2. Create a feature branch
  3. Make your changes with tests
  4. Update documentation (user-facing words follow docs/story.md)
  5. Submit a Pull Request against main

Releases ship from main and are published to npm.

See Development Guide for contribution workflow.

License

Claude-Mem is licensed under the Apache License 2.0.

We chose Apache-2.0 because durable agentic memory should be easy to embed in developer tools, local agents, MCP servers, enterprise systems, robotics stacks, and production agent harnesses.

See the LICENSE file for full details. See docs/license.md and docs/ip-boundary.md for licensing scope and the open/commercial boundary.

Support

  • Documentation: docs/
  • Issues: GitHub Issues
  • Repository: github.com/thedotmack/claude-mem
  • Official X Account: @Claude_Memory
  • Official Discord: Join Discord
  • Author: Alex Newman (@thedotmack)

Built with Claude Agent SDK | Works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode and more | Made with TypeScript

What About CMEM?

CMEM is a token created by a 3rd party but officially embraced by the creator of Claude-Mem (Alex Newman, @thedotmack). The token acts as a community catalyst for growth and a vehicle for bringing CMEM to the developers and knowledge workers that need it most.

item.title: NationalSecurityAgency/ghidra
item.description:
Ghidra is a software reverse engineering (SRE) framework

Ghidra Software Reverse Engineering Framework

Ghidra is a software reverse engineering (SRE) framework created and maintained by the National Security Agency Research Directorate. This framework includes a suite of full-featured, high-end software analysis tools that enable users to analyze compiled code on a variety of platforms including Windows, macOS, and Linux. Capabilities include disassembly, assembly, decompilation, graphing, and scripting, along with hundreds of other features. Ghidra supports a wide variety of processor instruction sets and executable formats and can be run in both user-interactive and automated modes. Users may also develop their own Ghidra extension components and/or scripts using Java or Python.

In support of NSA's Cybersecurity mission, Ghidra was built to solve scaling and teaming problems on complex SRE efforts, and to provide a customizable and extensible SRE research platform. NSA has applied Ghidra SRE capabilities to a variety of problems that involve analyzing malicious code and generating deep insights for SRE analysts who seek a better understanding of potential vulnerabilities in networks and systems.

If you are a U.S. citizen interested in projects like this, to develop Ghidra and other cybersecurity tools for NSA to help protect our nation and its allies, consider applying for a career with us.

Security Warning

WARNING: There are known security vulnerabilities within certain versions of Ghidra. Before proceeding, please read through Ghidra's Security Advisories for a better understanding of how you might be impacted.

Install

To install an official pre-built multi-platform Ghidra release:

  • Install JDK 25 64-bit
  • Download a Ghidra release file
    • NOTE: The official multi-platform release file is named ghidra_<version>_<release>_<date>.zip which can be found under the "Assets" drop-down. Downloading either of the files named "Source Code" is not correct for this step.
  • Extract the Ghidra release file
    • NOTE: Do not extract on top of an existing installation
  • Launch Ghidra: ./ghidraRun (ghidraRun.bat for Windows)
    • or launch PyGhidra: ./support/pyghidraRun (support\pyghidraRun.bat for Windows)

For additional information and troubleshooting tips about installing and running a Ghidra release, please refer to the Getting Started document which can be found at the root of a Ghidra installation directory.

Build

To create the latest development build for your platform from this source repository:

Install build tools:
  • JDK 25 64-bit
  • Gradle 9.1.0+ (or provided Gradle wrapper if Internet connection is available)
  • Python3 (version 3.9 to 3.15) with bundled pip
  • GCC or Clang, and make (Linux/macOS-only)
  • Microsoft Visual Studio 2017+ or Microsoft C++ Build Tools with the following components installed (Windows-only):
    • MSVC
    • Windows SDK
    • C++ ATL
Download and extract the source:

Download from GitHub

unzip ghidra-master
cd ghidra-master

NOTE: Instead of downloading the compressed source, you may instead want to clone the GitHub repository: git clone https://github.com/NationalSecurityAgency/ghidra.git

Download additional build dependencies into source repository:

NOTE: If an Internet connection is available and you did not install Gradle, the ./gradlew (or gradlew.bat) command may be used in place of the gradle command in the following instructions.

gradle -I gradle/support/fetchDependencies.gradle
Create development build:
gradle buildGhidra

The compressed development build will be located at build/dist/.

For more detailed information on building Ghidra, please read the Developer's Guide.

For issues building, please check the Known Issues section for possible solutions.

Develop

User Scripts and Extensions

Ghidra installations support users writing custom scripts and extensions via the GhidraDev plugin for Eclipse. The plugin and its corresponding instructions can be found within a Ghidra release at Extensions/Eclipse/GhidraDev/ or at this link. Alternatively, Visual Studio Code may be used to edit scripts by clicking the Visual Studio Code icon in the Script Manager. Fully-featured Visual Studio Code projects can be created from a Ghidra CodeBrowser window at Tools -> Create VSCode Module project.

NOTE: Both the GhidraDev plugin for Eclipse and Visual Studio Code integrations only support developing against fully built Ghidra installations which can be downloaded from the Releases page.

Advanced Development

To develop the Ghidra tool itself, it is highly recommended to use Eclipse, which the Ghidra development process has been highly customized for.

Install build and development tools:
  • Follow the above build instructions so the build completes without errors
  • Install Eclipse IDE for Java Developers
Prepare the development environment:
gradle prepdev eclipse buildNatives
Import Ghidra projects into Eclipse:
  • File -> Import...
  • General | Existing Projects into Workspace
  • Select root directory to be your downloaded or cloned ghidra source repository
  • Check Search for nested projects
  • Click Finish

When Eclipse finishes building the projects, Ghidra can be launched and debugged with the provided Ghidra Eclipse run configuration.

For more detailed information on developing Ghidra, please read the Developer's Guide.

Contribute

If you would like to contribute bug fixes, improvements, and new features back to Ghidra, please take a look at our Contributor's Guide to see how you can participate in this open source project.

item.title: pbakaus/impeccable
item.description:
The design vocabulary for your coding agent. Steer with polish and bolder, review with critique and audit, catch AI slop before it ships.

https://impeccable.style

Impeccable

The design vocabulary for your coding agent. Steer with polish and bolder, review with critique and audit, and catch AI slop before it ships.

From your project root:

npx impeccable install

Reload your coding tool, then run /impeccable init in your agent ($impeccable init on Codex).

Works with Claude Code, Cursor, Codex CLI, GitHub Copilot, Devin, Replit Agent, Gemini CLI, Grok Build, OpenCode, Google Antigravity, Kiro, Trae, Rovo Dev, Qoder, Mistral Vibe, Pi, Hermes Agent, DeepSeek Harness, and Veto. Full docs live at impeccable.style/docs.

Without Impeccable With Impeccable

Same model (Fable 5.1), same brief: a fourteen-room family guesthouse on the Ligurian coast. Without Impeccable, it builds the tasteful default: cream page, thin serif, italic accent, pill buttons. With it, the page is built around one picture: the house at night, seen from the water.

For a full project, see the Neo Mirai case study: a conference site taken from mockup to shipped page.

Why

Inter for everything. Purple-to-blue gradients. Cards nested in cards, gray text on colored backgrounds, a rounded-square icon tile above every heading. Ask an agent for a page with no other guidance and these show up again and again, across models and projects.

  • Words for what you want. "Make it pop" leaves your agent to guess. /impeccable bolder the pricing cards loads a playbook written for that one move and points it at one target.
  • A reviewer. critique scores the design against usability heuristics and ranks what to fix first. audit checks accessibility, performance, theming, and responsive behavior, with findings ranked P0 (blocking) to P3 (polish).
  • A slop detector. 62 deterministic rules flag the tells above, plus quality problems like cramped padding and skipped headings. No LLM, no API key.

Impeccable is strongest on interfaces that already exist: point it at a page or a component and iterate. It builds new pages too; see Build something new for how to get the most out of that harder mode. To start, pick one component:

/impeccable critique the pricing cards

How it works

Run /impeccable init once per project. It reads your code, asks only what it can't infer (who the product is for, what it needs to do, the constraints), and writes PRODUCT.md. Every later command reads it. Run /impeccable document to capture your existing visual system in DESIGN.md, so changes stay on-brand. More on context files.

Then name a command and a target:

/impeccable critique the onboarding flow
/impeccable quieter the landing page
/impeccable polish settings
/impeccable harden checkout

Or just describe what you want: /impeccable redo this hero section. Narrow targets get better results; a single section reviewed closely beats a whole page at a glance. Pin a command you use often with /impeccable pin audit to get /audit as its own shortcut.

24 commands

Commands
Steer bolder amplifies safe designs · quieter tones down loud ones · distill removes what the page doesn't need · colorize brings color to a gray interface · typeset fixes fonts, hierarchy, and sizing · layout fixes spacing and rhythm · animate adds transitions and interaction feedback · delight adds personality · overdrive goes for shaders, spring physics, and scroll-driven effects
Review critique is a scored UX review · audit is a technical quality report
Finish polish is the final pass before shipping · harden covers errors, i18n, overflow, and edge cases · clarify rewrites unclear copy · adapt handles screen sizes and devices · optimize fixes loading and rendering performance · onboard designs first-run flows and empty states
Iterate live live lets you pick an element in the browser and cycle through variants · generate produces variants of a named element without manual picking
Plan and set up shape plans UX before code · init writes PRODUCT.md · document writes DESIGN.md · extract pulls repeated patterns into your design system

The 24th, craft, is a deprecated alias for a plain build request. Type /impeccable alone to see the list in your agent. Each command has its own page: impeccable.style/docs.

On Codex, open /skills or type $impeccable instead of the slash command.

Live mode

/impeccable live opens your running dev server with an overlay. Select an element, pick a direction, and Impeccable hot-swaps variants in place. Accept one and it is written back to your source. It works with Vite, Next, SvelteKit, Astro, Nuxt, and plain HTML. Iterate in the browser.

Live mode edits a local checkout only; don't inject it into a deployed site or weaken a production CSP to make it work. Applying copy edits runs your package.json's optional impeccable:manual-edit-validate script with your permissions, so review it before using live mode in an unfamiliar repo.

Apply sends staged copy edits to your chat agent while a live session is polling. If none has polled in the last minute, it runs the codex CLI from your PATH instead (or claude when codex is missing), with approvals, permission checks, and sandboxing off (--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox or --permission-mode bypassPermissions) and your environment inherited. Its prompt carries the staged edits, the edited elements' HTML and nearby text, the page URL, and candidate source paths. Set IMPECCABLE_LIVE_COPY_AGENT=chat in the environment that starts live mode to keep Apply in your chat session, or off to disable Apply. The server reads it once at startup.

Three ways to run the detector

In your agent. The design hook scans every UI file your agent edits and hands the findings back before the agent calls the work done. This is where most slop gets caught: without the hook, the detector only runs when someone remembers to run it. It's available on Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, GitHub Copilot, Grok Build, and Hermes Agent, and the installer sets it up. Say yes. Automatic design checks.

In CI or your terminal. The CLI needs no agent:

npx impeccable detect src/                   # scan a directory
npx impeccable detect https://example.com    # scan a rendered page (uses your installed Chrome or Edge)
npx impeccable detect --json .               # machine-readable output
npx impeccable detect --github src/          # GitHub Actions annotations
npx impeccable detect --list-rules           # every rule with its id and description

Source files like JSX and TSX get the pattern rules only. Rules that need a rendered page, such as low contrast and tiny text, run when you scan a URL, so point the CLI at your dev server too: npx impeccable detect http://localhost:5173.

Exit code 2 means findings, 1 means a target couldn't be scanned. To allow your brand font everywhere, run npx impeccable ignores add-value overused-font Inter --reason "Brand font". To turn a rule off for one file, add a comment: <!-- impeccable-disable overused-font: exported brand doc -->. Run a detector scan · Configuration and ignores.

In your browser. The Chrome extension overlays the same findings on any live page, yours or anyone else's. Review with a visual overlay.

Installation

npx impeccable install

The installer detects your coding tools, asks whether to install for this project or globally, and offers the design hook where your tool supports one. Accept the hook. Reload your tool afterward. npx impeccable update refreshes an existing install. For scripts, pass --providers=claude,codex,cursor and --scope=project|global.

Three tools need one more step before the hook runs. In Codex, open /hooks and approve the project hook (again after an update that changes it). In Grok Build, run /hooks-trust or launch with --trust. In Hermes Agent, the hook is a plugin: run hermes plugins enable impeccable-design-hook once. Allow the hook in your harness.

Node is only needed for npx. The skill itself runs a self-contained engine binary that ships next to it or downloads once into ~/.impeccable/bin/.

Claude Code, Copilot, and Grok plugins

Claude Code: /plugin marketplace add pbakaus/impeccable, then open /plugin and install Impeccable.

GitHub Copilot in VS Code: install Impeccable from the Visual Studio Marketplace or run code --install-extension renaissance-geek.impeccable. Needs VS Code 1.109.3+, Copilot Chat, and a trusted workspace. It installs the skill without the hook. Details.

Grok Build: grok plugin install pbakaus/impeccable#plugin --trust installs the skill, agents, and hook.

Git submodule (a pinned version for the whole team) 
git submodule add https://github.com/pbakaus/impeccable vendor/impeccable
npx impeccable link --source=vendor/impeccable --providers=claude,cursor

Commit .gitmodules, the submodule, and the generated links. Teammates run git submodule update --init --recursive. To upgrade, run git submodule update --remote vendor/impeccable, rerun the link command, and commit. Linking installs skills, not hooks. Existing skill folders stay put unless you pass --force.

Manual copy, no Node required

Download the ZIP for your tool from impeccable.style, or clone this repo: each tool's build is committed at the repo root. Copy skills/impeccable from the folder below into the same place in your project, or into the global folder.

Tool Repo folder Global skills folder
Claude Code .claude/ ~/.claude/skills/
Cursor .cursor/
Codex CLI, Replit Agent .agents/ ~/.agents/skills/
Devin .devin/ ${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-$HOME/.config}/devin/skills/
GitHub Copilot .github/
Gemini CLI .gemini/
Google Antigravity .agent/ ~/.gemini/config/skills/
OpenCode .opencode/
Grok Build .grok/ ~/.grok/skills/
Hermes Agent .hermes/ ${HERMES_HOME:-$HOME/.hermes}/skills/
DeepSeek Harness .dsh/ ${DSH_HOME:-$HOME/.dsh}/skills/
Pi .pi/
Qoder .qoder/ ~/.qoder/skills/
Rovo Dev .rovodev/ ~/.rovodev/skills/
Mistral Vibe .vibe/ ~/.vibe/skills/
Trae .trae/ ~/.trae/skills/

For example: mkdir -p your-project/.claude/skills && cp -r .claude/skills/impeccable your-project/.claude/skills/.

Notes:

  • A manual copy skips the design hook and subagents. Run npx impeccable install to get them; it writes each tool's hook pointing at the right skill path.
  • OpenCode also needs .opencode/commands/impeccable.md copied into your project's .opencode/commands/ to provide /impeccable.
  • Hermes asks you to trust project-local skills once: run hermes skills trust from the project root. Global installs need no trust step.
  • Cursor and Gemini CLI may need Agent Skills enabled in settings. See the Cursor and Gemini CLI skills docs.
  • Restart Trae after copying.
  • impeccable install and update manage a DeepSeek Harness global copy only when DSH_HOME is inside your home directory.

Project files and git

Impeccable writes its working files under .impeccable/. A few are shared project artifacts and belong in the repo: config.json, live/config.json, design.json, surfaces/*.md, and critique/*.md. Keep PRODUCT.md and DESIGN.md in the repo too. The rest is screenshots, caches, and runtime state.

Copy the .gitignore entries 
# impeccable-ignore-start
# Ephemeral output, runtime state, and per-dev overrides.
# The **/ prefix covers .impeccable at the repo root or in a nested workspace.
# Shared artifacts stay tracked: config.json, live/config.json,
# design.json, surfaces/*.md, critique/*.md.
**/.impeccable/config.local.json
**/.impeccable/hook.cache.json
**/.impeccable/hook.pending.json
**/.impeccable/*.png
**/.impeccable/review/
**/.impeccable/questions/
**/.impeccable/live/server.json
**/.impeccable/live/sessions/
**/.impeccable/live/previews/
**/.impeccable/live/annotations/
**/.impeccable/live/cache/
**/.impeccable/live/manual-edit-apply-transaction.json
**/.impeccable/live/manual-edit-events.jsonl
**/.impeccable/live/manual-edit-evidence/
**/.impeccable/live/pending-manual-edits.json
**/.impeccable/live/deferred-svelte-component-accepts.json
**/.impeccable/live/*.png
# impeccable-ignore-end

The folders that hold decision-round state (.impeccable/questions/, .impeccable/mocks/worlds/) also ignore themselves. A .gitignore can't untrack a file git already tracks; if you committed one earlier, run git rm --cached <path>.

Good to know

Build path. For new landing pages and showcase surfaces, Impeccable can generate a full-fidelity comp first and build to match it (bolder, slower), or build straight in code (leaner, faster). App screens and documents are always built in code. init asks once and saves the answer as buildPath in .impeccable/config.json; the decision page lets you override it for one session. The choice only appears when your harness can generate images. Image generation · Configuration.

Hooks run outside model approval. In Claude Code, installed command hooks run even when you deny the model's own commands, so the first edit can download the engine. Review installed hooks before unattended runs, or pass --settings '{"disableAllHooks": true}' to turn them off for a run. The installer leaves hook entries it didn't add alone.

Something broken? /impeccable doctor finds stale context files, unused settings, and broken hooks. Fix setup problems.

Telemetry. When a new design starts, the skill fetches a set of visual directions from the impeccable.style catalog. Turning telemetry off doesn't stop that request; it stops the anonymous record of which directions were shown and which one you picked, which is how the catalog learns what works. Your project name, files, code, and PRODUCT.md are never sent. Disable telemetry with npx impeccable telemetry off, DO_NOT_TRACK=1, or "telemetry": false in .impeccable/config.json for the whole project. The full list of what is sent is on the privacy page.

Community

  • Issues for bugs, questions, and ideas. Outside contributions start with an issue; see DEVELOP.md.
  • Changelog for what shipped.
  • Follow @pbakaus for release notes and new rules.
